title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
extended_summary:
The paper addresses how widely large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, LLaMA, Gemini, and Bing Copilot are being used by secondary students, despite school restrictions and concerns about cheating, hallucinations, and unequal access. The authors aim to understand prevalence of use, subjects in which students use LLMs, student satisfaction and concerns, school policy strictness, and demographic or access-related differences in usage.

The study used a survey approach rather than testing a classroom intervention. The survey was distributed through Centiment, Google Forms, local tutoring programs, and social media. It collected responses from 306 students in grades 6 through 12 across 43 U.S. states, including students from public, private, charter, and homeschool backgrounds and with varying levels of access to technology.

The main findings were that 71% of respondents had used LLMs at least once, with usage relatively consistent across grades 7–12, and 9% reporting daily use. Students reported using LLMs across multiple subjects, including language arts, history, math, foreign languages, and STEM. Students found LLMs useful for tasks such as writing support and explaining complex topics, but also reported concerns about inaccurate answers, hallucinations, weak reasoning, and overreliance.

The authors conclude that LLM use among secondary students is already widespread and likely to increase. They argue that restrictions alone are unlikely to be effective and propose student-adapted LLMs, AI tutors, and “AI classrooms” as possible ways to improve learning support and reduce inequities. They also highlight access gaps, noting higher reported LLM use among students in more technologically advanced states, private school students, and students able to pay for premium models.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General-purpose large language model chatbots used for text generation, question answering, problem solving, and schoolwork assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed as a category of LLM tools used by secondary students for schoolwork assistance across multiple subjects.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of n=306 middle and high school students, 71% reported having used LLMs at least once, and 9% reported using them daily. Usage was described as consistent across grades 7 to 12 despite generally restrictive school policies.
findings.measure: Self-reported LLM usage frequency among secondary students

findings.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs across school subjects, including language arts, history, foreign languages, STEM, and math; 28% of students used LLMs for math. Among LLM users, 57% found them useful for writing text and 43% found them useful for math and STEM questions, while open-ended responses noted both simplification of complex topics and risks of inaccuracy or overreliance.
findings.measure: Self-reported subject use and perceived usefulness for writing, math, and STEM

findings.finding_summary: Students rated school policy strictness around LLM help at an average of 3.48 on a 1–5 scale, where 5 indicated severe punishment. They rated ethical concern at an average of 2.83 on a 1–5 scale, and the paper reports that usage persisted despite these concerns.
findings.measure: Student ratings of school policy strictness and ethical concern about LLM use

findings.finding_summary: The survey found access-related usage gaps: 80.2% of students in the five highest-ranking states on the State Technology and Science Index had used LLMs, compared with 64.3% of students in other states. Private school students reported 76.7% LLM usage versus 71.3% among public school students, and among the 17 participants with paid model access, all except one reported using LLMs at least 2–3 times per week.
findings.measure: Self-reported LLM usage by state technology ranking, school type, and paid model access

findings.finding_summary: When asked about desired improvements, 51% of respondents wanted more coherent responses, more accurate answers, and better ability to address complex questions. Only 3% wanted no modifications, and 20% wanted better emotional understanding and conversations, indicating dissatisfaction with current LLM reliability for schoolwork.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s general-purpose conversational LLM product for generating text, answering questions, and assisting with problem solving.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as a named LLM used by secondary students for schoolwork; the paper reports ChatGPT-specific adoption prevalence.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that 84% of LLM users in the survey used ChatGPT, which translates to 60% of all respondents. The authors compare this with a reported 43% ChatGPT usage rate among U.S. young adults aged 18–29 from a February poll.
findings.measure: Self-reported ChatGPT use among LLM users and all respondents

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google’s general-purpose Gemini family of large language models and chatbot systems for multimodal and text-based assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed as one of the LLMs included in the survey of secondary student use; no Gemini-specific results were reported.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta’s LLaMA family of large language models for text generation and language-based assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed as one of the LLMs included in the survey of secondary student use; no LLaMA-specific results were reported.

identified_tools.name: Bing Copilot
identified_tools.description: Microsoft’s Bing Copilot conversational AI assistant for search, question answering, and generative assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Listed as one of the LLMs included in the survey of secondary student use; no Bing Copilot-specific results were reported.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey of n=306 U.S. secondary students using descriptive statistics and open-ended responses. It is empirical but non-causal, with acknowledged accessibility and sampling limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports descriptive adoption and perception results rather than causal effects on student learning. Reported student views are mixed, with usefulness for writing and STEM alongside concerns about hallucinations, incorrect answers, ethics, and access gaps.
